title: He dug a pit of mud to practice high jump. He won Paralympic gold anyway. October 18, 2026.
excerpt: From Delhi's first-ever police record to an AI assistant for 10,000 Indian school labs, to the country's first homemade hydrogen train - October 18's five stories are about building the institution, tool, or body you need, even when no one hands it to you.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is about constructing something from almost nothing - a record-keeping system starting from one small theft, an engineering career starting from a stadium food-service job, a teaching tool built for labs that already needed support, a train engineered at home instead of imported, and a landing pit dug out of mud because no mattress was available.

October 18, 1861: Delhi's first-ever police complaint was written down - in Urdu and Persian

Sabzi Mandi Police Station registered Delhi's first First Information Report, a theft complaint worth about 45 annas, months after the Police Act of 1861 created the modern Indian police force. A copy survives today at the Delhi Police Museum.

She arrived in the US at 21 with little money, working as a stadium food server to pay for school. Forbes just named her one of the world's top innovators at 53

Yamini Rangan, CEO of HubSpot since 2021, was named to Forbes' 2026 '50 Over 50' Innovation list, having guided the software company past $3 billion in annual revenue after completing her engineering degree in India and an MBA at UC Berkeley.

An India-born CEO just built an AI tool for 10,000 Indian school labs

At India's AI Impact Summit in February 2026, Google - led by India-born CEO Sundar Pichai - partnered with NITI Aayog's Atal Innovation Mission to launch ATL Saathi, a Gemini-powered teaching assistant now scaling across India's Atal Tinkering Labs.

India just ran its first homemade hydrogen train

India's first domestically built hydrogen-powered passenger train was flagged off July 17, 2026 on the Jind-Sonipat route in Haryana, running on a 1,200 kW fuel cell system with its only emission being water vapour.

He dug a pit of mud to practice high jump. He won Paralympic gold anyway

Praveen Kumar, born with a congenital leg condition to a poor farming family near Jewar, dug his own training pit during COVID lockdowns and went on to win silver at Tokyo 2020 and gold at Paris 2024 in the T64 high jump, both at Asian-record heights.

Five stories, one pattern: a record system that started with one small theft, a career built from a food-service job into global software leadership, a teaching tool built for labs that needed support, a train engineered at home rather than imported, and a landing pit dug from mud that turned into an Asian record.
